content: 1. If there is no fetal movement or if the membranes have ruptured without labor, assess the situation by asking questions, checking medical records, and performing a physical examination. Look for signs, classify the condition, and provide appropriate treatment and advice. 2. If the patient has a fever or experiences burning during urination, ask if they have had a fever. If there is a history of fever or the patient feels hot, measure their axillary temperature, check for a stiff neck, and assess for lethargy. If signs of a very severe febrile disease are present, insert an IV line and administer fluids slowly. Provide appropriate IM/IV antibiotics, artemether or quinine IM, and glucose. Refer the patient urgently to a hospital. 3. For upper urinary tract infections, administer appropriate IM/IV antibiotics and oral antimalarials if necessary. Refer the patient urgently to a hospital. 4. For malaria, confirm the diagnosis with parasitological testing. Administer appropriate oral antimalarials. If there is no improvement within two days or the condition worsens, refer the patient to a hospital. 5. For lower urinary tract infections, provide appropriate oral antibiotics and encourage the patient to drink more fluids. If there is no improvement within two days or the condition worsens, refer the patient to a hospital. 6. If the patient reports vaginal discharge, ask about changes in the discharge, vulvar itching, or urinary problems in their partner. If the partner is present, and the patient is comfortable, ask the partner about urethral discharge, pus, or burning during urination. Examine the vaginal discharge for abnormalities in amount, color, and odor. 7. If abnormal vaginal discharge is observed, consider possible gonorrhea or chlamydia infection. Administer appropriate oral antibiotics to the patient and their partner. Counsel on safer sex practices, including condom use. 8. If the discharge resembles curd-like material, suspect a possible Candida infection. Provide clotrimazole and counsel on safer sex practices. 9. If the discharge suggests bacterial or trichomonas infection, administer metronidazole to the patient and counsel on safer sex practices. 10. If signs suggest severe or advanced HIV infection, ask about weight loss, diarrhea lasting more than one month, fever lasting more than one month, cough lasting more than one month, or difficulty breathing. Assess for high-risk factors such as occupational exposure or multiple sexual partners. Look for visible wasting, skin rashes, blisters along the ribs, enlarged lymph nodes, oral ulcers, or abnormal vaginal discharge. Refer the patient to a hospital for further assessment if there is a strong likelihood of severe or advanced symptomatic HIV infection. 11. If the patient smokes, uses alcohol or drugs, or has a history of violence, assess dependency on tobacco or alcohol. Counsel on stopping tobacco use and avoiding second-hand smoke. For alcohol or drug abuse, refer the patient to specialized care providers. Provide counseling on violence if necessary. 12. If the patient has a cough or difficulty breathing, ask about the duration of symptoms, chest pain, or blood in sputum. Check for breathlessness and listen for wheezing. If fever exceeds 38°C and breathlessness is present, suspect possible pneumonia. Administer the first dose of appropriate IM/IV antibiotics and refer urgently to a hospital. 13. If the patient has been coughing or experiencing breathing difficulty for more than three weeks, or if there is blood in sputum or wheezing, suspect possible chronic lung disease. Refer the patient to a hospital for assessment. 14. For upper respiratory tract infections, advise safe and soothing remedies. Counsel on stopping smoking and avoiding second-hand smoke. 15. If the patient is taking anti-tuberculosis drugs, determine the duration of treatment. If the regimen includes streptomycin, refer the patient to a district hospital for treatment revision, as streptomycin is ototoxic to the fetus. If the regimen does not include streptomycin, reassure the patient that the drugs are safe for the baby and encourage adherence to treatment. 16. If the patient’s sputum is TB-positive within two months of delivery, plan to provide INH prophylaxis to the newborn. Reinforce advice on HIV testing and counseling. Counsel on stopping smoking and avoiding second-hand smoke. Advise screening of immediate family members and close contacts for tuberculosis. 17. Provide preventive measures during antenatal care visits. Administer tetanus toxoid if due, and plan for subsequent doses. Provide a three-month supply of iron, aspirin, calcium, and ART if prescribed, and counsel on adherence and safety. Administer mebendazole once in the second or third trimester. Provide intermittent preventive treatment for malaria and encourage sleeping under insecticide-treated bed nets. 18. During the first antenatal visit, develop a birth and emergency plan. Counsel on nutrition, exclusive breastfeeding, and avoiding tobacco, alcohol, and drug use. Advise on safer sex practices, including condom use. 19. During all visits, review and update the birth and emergency plan. Advise on when to seek care, including routine visits, follow-up visits, and danger signs. In the third trimester, counsel on family planning and abstinence from harmful substances. Record all visits and treatments provided. 20. Counsel on nutrition by advising the patient to eat a variety of healthy foods, such as meat, fish, oils, nuts, seeds, cereals, beans, vegetables, cheese, and milk. Spend more time on nutrition counseling for very thin, adolescent, or HIV-infected women. Address any food taboos and involve family members in ensuring the patient eats well and avoids hard physical work. 21. Advise on self-care during pregnancy, including taking iron tablets, resting, avoiding heavy lifting, sleeping under insecticide-treated bed nets, and practicing safer sex. Counsel on avoiding alcohol and smoking and not taking medications unless prescribed. 22. For family planning, explain the importance of starting early discussions about contraception. Inform the patient that pregnancy can occur as soon as four weeks after delivery if not exclusively breastfeeding. Advise waiting at least two years before trying to conceive again for the health of the mother and baby. Provide information on contraceptive methods and arrange for counseling if needed. 23. For facility delivery, explain the importance of delivering in a facility due to the unpredictability of complications. Discuss the availability of staff, equipment, and drugs in facilities, as well as the need for ARV treatment for HIV-infected women and their babies during childbirth. Review arrangements for delivery, including transportation, costs, and support during labor. 24. For home delivery with a skilled attendant, review the necessary preparations, including identifying a companion during labor, ensuring someone is available to help with household responsibilities, and having the maternal record ready. Discuss the supplies needed for a clean and safe delivery, such as clean cloths, blankets, soap, and clean water. 25. Advise on labor signs, such as bloody sticky discharge, painful contractions every 20 minutes or less, and ruptured membranes. Emphasize the importance of going to a facility or contacting a skilled birth attendant immediately if these signs occur. 26. Discuss danger signs during pregnancy, such as vaginal bleeding, convulsions, severe headaches with blurred vision, fever with weakness, severe abdominal pain, and fast or difficult breathing. Advise seeking immediate care if these signs are present. 27. Discuss emergency preparedness, including where to go, how to get there, costs, and support during labor. Encourage the patient to seek help from the community if needed.
